from manim import *

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

class Section2Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        self.setup_layout("The Two 'Magical' Operations", [
            "Vector spaces require two fundamental operations.",
            "First, we must be able to add vectors.",
            "Second, we must allow scalar multiplication."
        ])
        
        # --- Preparation ---
        # Vectors (arrows)
        v1 = Arrow(ORIGIN, RIGHT*1.5 + UP*1.0, color=WHITE, buff=0)
        v2 = Arrow(ORIGIN, RIGHT*1.0 - UP*0.5, color=WHITE, buff=0)
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        # Vector spaces require two fundamental operations.
        self.play(self.lecture[0].animate.set_color("#FFFFFF"))
        self.play(Create(v1), Create(v2))
        lbl1 = Text("Operations", font_size=20, color=WHITE)
        self.place_at_grid(lbl1, 'B2')
        self.play(Write(lbl1))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        # First, we must be able to add vectors.
        self.play(self.lecture[1].animate.set_color("#FFD700"))
        
        # Addition: v1 + v2
        v_sum = Arrow(ORIGIN, v1.end + v2.end, color="#FFD700", buff=0)
        v2_shifted = Arrow(v1.end, v1.end + v2.get_vector(), color=WHITE, buff=0)
        
        self.play(FadeOut(lbl1), FadeOut(v2))
        self.play(Create(v2_shifted), Create(v_sum))
        
        lbl2 = Text("Vector Addition", font_size=20, color="#FFD700")
        self.place_at_grid(lbl2, 'C3')
        self.play(Write(lbl2))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        # Second, we must allow scalar multiplication.
        self.play(self.lecture[2].animate.set_color("#00CED1"))
        
        # Scalar mult: v1 * 2
        v1_scaled = Arrow(ORIGIN, v1.get_vector()*2, color="#00CED1", buff=0)
        
        self.play(FadeOut(v2_shifted), FadeOut(v_sum), FadeOut(lbl2))
        self.play(Transform(v1, v1_scaled))
        
        lbl3 = Text("Scalar Multiplication", font_size=20, color="#00CED1")
        self.place_at_grid(lbl3, 'D3')
        self.play(Write(lbl3))
        self.wait(1)

class Section5Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        self.setup_layout("The Power of Generalization", [
            "Abstract vector spaces unify diverse fields.",
            "They connect physics, AI, and signal processing.",
            "Generalization simplifies solving complex problems."
        ])
        
        # Elements
        physics_icon = Circle(radius=0.5, color=BLUE).add(Text("P", font_size=24))
        ai_icon = Square(side_length=0.8, color=GREEN).add(Text("AI", font_size=24))
        signals_icon = Star(n=5, color=RED).add(Text("S", font_size=24))
        core = Circle(radius=0.7, color=YELLOW, fill_opacity=0.3)
        core_label = Text("Vector Space", font_size=20, color=WHITE)
        
        icons = VGroup(physics_icon, ai_icon, signals_icon)
        
        # Positions
        self.place_at_grid(physics_icon, "B2", scale_factor=0.8)
        self.place_at_grid(ai_icon, "B5", scale_factor=0.8)
        self.place_at_grid(signals_icon, "E3", scale_factor=0.8)
        self.place_at_grid(core, "D3", scale_factor=1.0)
        core_label.next_to(core, DOWN, buff=0.1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[0].animate.set_color("#FFFFFF"))
        self.play(FadeIn(physics_icon), FadeIn(ai_icon), FadeIn(signals_icon))
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[1].animate.set_color("#FFFF00"))
        lines = VGroup(
            Line(physics_icon.get_center(), core.get_center(), color=YELLOW),
            Line(ai_icon.get_center(), core.get_center(), color=YELLOW),
            Line(signals_icon.get_center(), core.get_center(), color=YELLOW)
        )
        self.play(Create(lines), FadeIn(core), FadeIn(core_label))
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[2].animate.set_color("#FFD700"))
        self.play(Indicate(core), core.animate.set_color(GOLD).set_fill(opacity=0.6))
        self.wait(2)

sections.title: From Concrete to Abstract (0:00-1:00)
sections.content: Recall 2D/3D Euclidean vectors (arrows with length and direction). Introduce the 'Abstraction Step': If we can add and scale arrows, can we do the same with other things? Define a Vector Space as a set of 'objects' (vectors) that satisfy 8 specific rules (axioms) regardless of what the objects 'look' like.
sections.example: Visual transition: A 2D arrow morphs into a complex mathematical function or a sound wave, showing that they all obey the same addition rules.

sections.title: The Two 'Magical' Operations (1:00-2:15)
sections.content: Focus on the closure properties: Vector Addition (u+v) and Scalar Multiplication (cv). These are the requirements for a system to be a 'Vector Space'. Use a visual 'Sandbox' metaphor where any combination of elements must stay inside the sandbox.
sections.example: An animated character 'Chef' mixing ingredients (vectors). If he mixes 'Red Sauce' and 'Blue Sauce', he gets 'Purple Sauce' (Addition). If he doubles the amount of ingredients, it's still 'Sauce' (Scalar Multiplication).

sections.title: Defining the 'Rules of the Game' (2:15-3:30)
sections.content: Briefly highlight key axioms: Commutativity (u+v = v+u), Associativity, and the existence of the Zero Vector. Explain that these aren't just arbitrary rules; they are the fundamental 'structural blueprint' that makes linear algebra work.
sections.example: A visual puzzle where puzzle pieces (vectors) must fit together according to the axioms. If one rule is broken, the 'structure' collapses, demonstrating why these axioms are essential.

sections.title: Applications: The Zoo of Vectors (3:30-4:30)
sections.content: Show that the 'vectors' in an abstract space aren't just arrows. Examples: The set of all polynomials of degree ≤ 2, or the set of all continuous functions. This explains why engineers use vector spaces to analyze vibrations or signal processing.
sections.example: A 'Vector Zoo' animation: One cage holds 'Arrows', another 'Polynomials', and another 'Data Tables'. An inspector (the student) checks if each cage follows the 8 Axioms.

sections.title: Conclusion: The Power of Generalization (4:30-5:00)
sections.content: Summarize that abstract vector spaces allow us to solve complex problems in physics and AI using the same math used for basic 2D arrows. The abstraction is not meant to confuse, but to unify.
sections.example: Final screen shows a unified map connecting a physical bridge (structural engineering), a neural network (data science), and a musical instrument (wave analysis) all linked back to the 'Abstract Vector Space' core.
